solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: That is no time for date from the past

indicators.note: 'no' says the following item is missing from what came before

parts.note: 'that is' translates the Latin id est, written as one run of letters

explanation.surface: Someone declares that there is no time left for a date with an old flame.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin id est (that is) loses its final T, signalled by 'no time'. 'Date' is not a romantic appointment here but a day in the Roman calendar.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old Roman calendar these were a fixed day in each month, famous from the warning to Caesar about mid-March.

clue.text: Involved in mishap — a Cherokee Native American

indicators.note: letters that are involved in a phrase sit inside it, spanning the words

explanation.surface: A Cherokee person is caught up in some accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cherokee' tempts you to look for that tribe's name, but it only hosts the start of a different tribe's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the name of a group of Indigenous peoples of the American Southwest, so a member is a Native American.

clue.text: Setting with leaky moat round

indicators.note: a leaky container lets its contents escape and shift, so the letters of moat are rearranged

parts.note: a round object is a ball or globe, a sphere

explanation.surface: A castle's setting includes a moat that leaks all the way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setting' is the scene or mood of a story, not a jewel's mount; 'leaky' makes the moat's letters spill into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words can mean the mood or surroundings in which something takes place, as in a tense setting.

clue.text: Loosely a pure biting cold insight

indicators.note: something biting has its teeth around a piece, so these letters close around another
taken loosely, the letters of 'a pure' are allowed to rearrange freely

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A vague, pure flash of understanding about the biting cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loosely' rearranges A PURE to APERU, which 'biting' wraps around C (cold).
explanation.definitionFit: This French borrowing means a brief, illuminating comment or flash of understanding, a synonym of insight.

clue.text: Two pairs of smalls under a popular offer?

indicators.note: 'Two' asks for the following group to be written twice
in a down clue, a piece under another comes after it

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, so a pair of them is SS
IN means popular or fashionable

explanation.surface: A shop deal on underwear: two packs of pants for a bargain offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smalls' is British slang for underwear but here means small letters. In a down clue 'under' places a piece below another; 'Two' doubles the result. 'Offer' is read as one who offs, a killer.
explanation.definitionFit: To off someone is slang for killing them, so an offer in that playful sense is a professional killer.

clue.text: Brand has ears boxed

indicators.note: boxed means enclosed as in a box, so the letters sit inside the words has ears

explanation.surface: Someone gets their ears boxed, as a punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxed' looks like an anagram signal for EARS, but it means the answer is boxed inside 'has ears'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to burn a mark into something with a hot iron, as with cattle.

clue.text: Two gin cocktails with vermouth in that will get you lit up

definitions.text: that will get you lit up

indicators.note: one piece goes in another
cocktails are mixtures, so the letters are mixed
'Two' asks for the word gin to be taken twice

parts.note: IT is short for Italian vermouth, as in the drink gin and it

explanation.surface: A barman's tip: two gin cocktails with vermouth will get you drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin and it is a classic drink, it being short for Italian vermouth. 'cocktails' mixes each gin separately and 'in' puts the vermouth between them. 'Lit up' looks like drunk but means set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting something alight is what makes it burn, so this verb form describes what lights it up.

clue.text: Nonconformists uninhibited with Winnie but not in a bad way

parts.note: uninhibited means free of restraint

indicators.note: 'but not' removes the following item from what came before

parts.note: Winnie was the nickname of Winston Churchill
someone in a bad way is ill

explanation.surface: Some free-spirited dissenters side with Winston Churchill, though not unkindly.
explanation.walkthrough: Winston Churchill, the wartime prime minister, loses ILL ('in a bad way'), as signalled by 'but not'.
explanation.definitionFit: Protestant groups outside the established Church of England were known as Nonconformists, and this is one such body.

clue.text: Remove plant from container warehouse?

definitions.meaning: read as ..., to take a plant out of its pot
a storage building or store for goods

explanation.surface: A gardener removes a plant from its pot at a warehouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a playful coinage, de-pot, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A storage building for goods or vehicles, the sense used for a bus or rail yard.

clue.text: See 12
Retired copper about to block crusty offering a helping hand

indicators.note: to block something is to sit in its way, inside it

parts.note: a crusty person is bad-tempered, sour

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn, going back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: CU is the chemical symbol for copper
C is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A retired policeman is about to stop a grumpy old man helping out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal, and 'Retired' turns its symbol backwards. 'to block' puts copper and 'about' inside the crusty word.
explanation.definitionFit: This word means aid or relief given in a time of need, just as a helping hand is help given.

clue.text: Pin raises general malfunctions for Sky customer?

indicators.note: something that malfunctions goes wrong, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A general's pin badge somehow breaks the satellite TV for a subscriber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sky' looks like the British satellite TV broadcaster, whose subscribers are its customers, but it is the actual sky. 'malfunctions' rearranges all of PIN RAISES GENERAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pays to travel through the sky on a commercial flight is a customer of the sky, a playful paraphrase.

clue.text: Ring dropped from tug by pilot originally — idiot!

indicators.note: dropped from means removed from what follows

parts.note: a tug is a boat that tows, so a tower
O is shaped like a ring

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of pilot

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at a pilot who let a ring fall from his tugboat.
explanation.walkthrough: A tug is read as a tower, something that tows; 'dropped from' takes out O (ring) to leave TWER, then P from 'pilot originally'.
explanation.definitionFit: A silly or foolish person, a mild British insult equivalent to an idiot.

clue.text: Mattress can't be used in this condition — or carpeting

definitions.text: Mattress can't be used in this condition
definitions.meaning: ticking is the strong striped cotton covering a mattress; with it off, the mattress is unusable
a carpeting is a severe scolding, from being called onto the boss's carpet

explanation.surface: A warning about a mattress being unusable in its present state, or about a carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: Ticking is the striped fabric cover of a mattress, so its absence is the first reading. 'Carpeting' is British slang for a reprimand, not floor covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprimand is the same as a carpeting, both meaning a sharp telling-off from a superior.

clue.text: Kind of international organisation maybe winkles out hard line separately

parts.note: UN, the United Nations, is one example of an international organisation

indicators.note: out says these letters are removed
separately says the two removed letters are taken from different places, not side by side

parts.note: winkles are small edible sea snails, a kind of shellfish
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A worldwide body perhaps draws a firm line between different winkles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winkles' gives SHELLFISH; 'out' and 'separately' take H and an L from it at different points, leaving SELFISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Being generous and considerate of others is a core sense of kind, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Los Angeles detectives arresting Siberian run out to get result of tough workout?

indicators.note: arresting means holding, so these letters hold another set inside
out takes the following letter away

parts.note: Siberian conditions are arctic, freezing
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British police detectives

explanation.surface: Los Angeles police detain a fugitive Siberian, and the effort leaves them aching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes the run from Siberian's synonym, and 'arresting' has the Los Angeles abbreviation holding what is left, before the detectives follow. CID is the British police detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: This compound builds up in muscles during strenuous exercise and is blamed for stiffness afterwards.

clue.text: Counterfeit tobacco ruling covering Home Counties almost successful

indicators.note: covering means wrapped around another piece
something counterfeit is a fake made up from other material, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: SE, south-east, is where England's Home Counties around London lie

explanation.surface: A ruling on fake tobacco is extended to cover the area around London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counterfeit' rearranges TOBACCO RULING, and the result goes around SE ('covering'). The Home Counties are the English counties surrounding London.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom, from fairground prizes, describes a near miss that earns no reward, just short of success.

clue.text: Delinquent given nothing very strong before un-British drinking spree

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
FF is fortissimo in music, very loud or strong

indicators.note: un-British means the abbreviation for British is removed

parts.note: a bender is a drinking spree

explanation.surface: A young delinquent gets nothing but strong drink before an un-British boozing session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'un-British' takes B from BENDER (a drinking spree) to leave ENDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A delinquent is a person who breaks the law, so a lawbreaker, the same as this noun.

clue.text: End feud I fancy without resistance

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or imagined, so the letters are made over into another form

explanation.surface: A speaker thinks they can end a feud without any opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges END FEUD I.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not defied has met no challenge or opposition, so it stands without resistance.

clue.text: Smart Bernie Ecclestone making silly point possibly

parts.note: smart means fashionable, in
the long-time Formula One boss, read playfully as an F1 elder, with the figure 1 as letter I

explanation.surface: A well-dressed Bernie Ecclestone strikes a pose.
explanation.walkthrough: Bernie Ecclestone ran Formula One for decades and is its grand old man, an F1 elder. Silly point is a cricket fielding position very close to the batter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket's silly point stands near the bat, so a player placed there is an example of a close fielder.

clue.text: Put energy into endless barter in order to get discount

indicators.note: Put starts the instruction to place one piece in another
into names where the piece is put
putting into order means sorting the letters again
endless means without its last letter

parts.note: E is the physics abbreviation for energy

explanation.surface: Bring some energy to haggling and you might get a discount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims BARTER to BARTE, E (energy) is 'Put into' it, and 'in order' rearranges the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A partial refund or reduction on the price paid is a discount, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Kind of setter perhaps that's hopeless lush, icier with no clue

indicators.note: hopeless means in a mess, so the letters are jumbled
with no says the letters of clue are taken away from the mix

explanation.surface: A crossword setter is a hopeless, cold drunk who cannot write a clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like the puzzle compiler but is the dog. Jumble LUSH ICIER, remove the letters of CLUE ('with no'), and the five left make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A red-coated gun dog breed is named after this nationality, so it is one kind of setter.

clue.text: Prudence — popular previously and perfect

indicators.note: previously says the piece before it comes first

parts.note: popular means in, in fashion
prudence, in the sense of discretion, is tact

explanation.surface: A woman named Prudence, once popular and flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prudence' looks like a name but means tact.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perfect is undamaged and whole, the same as being untouched or complete.

clue.text: Wizard egg and alfalfa sandwiches

indicators.note: sandwiches means holds between, so the answer sits inside the words

explanation.surface: A wizard makes egg and alfalfa sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' looks like the food, but it is a verb: the words hold the name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the name of the wizard in Tolkien's The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.

clue.text: Open a pot of jam?

parts.note: jam is sold in a jar

explanation.surface: A request to open a jam pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open' looks like a verb but is an adjective, as for a door left partly open.
explanation.definitionFit: A door slightly open is described this way, a direct synonym for open.

clue.text: Celtic's torrent of words for football official

definitions.meaning: in Scots, a Celtic tongue's neighbour, the word means a noisy rush of chatter
Sepp ... was president of FIFA, football's world governing body

explanation.surface: A Celtic fan's rant at the referee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celtic' looks like the Glasgow football club but stands for Scottish usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepp Blatter headed FIFA from 1998 to 2015, a senior football administrator.

clue.text: Unusual pink

definitions.meaning: steak cooked lightly, still pink inside

explanation.definitionFit: The word means uncommon, and also describes meat lightly cooked so it stays red inside.

clue.text: Frank's a toff, being his own boss

parts.note: frank means open or free; the 's is read as is, a link
a toff is a posh gentleman, a gent

explanation.surface: Frank is a posh man who works for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name but means free. A toff is British slang for an upper-class man.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not bound by any contract or employer answers to nobody else, so is his own boss.

clue.text: Run home with dog

parts.note: at home means in
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A dog owner goes for a jog home with the dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like jogging but means run up, as a debt.
explanation.definitionFit: To run up a cost or run a risk is to bring it upon yourself, which is the meaning here.
